The abacus is one of the oldest known calculating tools, and its history spans several civilizations. The earliest counting boards appear in Mesopotamia around 2700 to 2300 BCE, where pebbles or tokens were moved in grooves or on flat surfaces to track quantities. The Sumerians and later Babylonians used a base-60 system that suited this kind of positional counting.

In the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, counting boards called *abax* or *abacus* held pebbles (*calculi*) in columns. Roman merchants and officials used small bronze versions, some with grooves for sliding counters, and these helped with trade, taxes, and military supply.

China developed the suanpan, a bead abacus with two beads above a divider and five below in each column, by at least the 12th century CE, and it is often dated to the Song or Yuan dynasty. Its layout let users carry out addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and even square and cube roots with fast, practiced hand movements. Chinese mathematicians wrote detailed manuals on its methods.

The Japanese soroban descended from the Chinese design. It uses one bead above the bar and four below in each column, which reduced the number of beads needed. It became standard in Japanese schools and commerce and remained in common use into the twentieth century.

Abacus use spread across Asia and, after European contact, returned to parts of Europe and Russia, where the schoty and similar frames were widely used. Even after mechanical and electronic calculators became common, the abacus continued to be taught in parts of Asia for mental arithmetic training.

The slide rule grew out of the logarithm. John Napier published logarithmic tables in 1614, and within a few years English mathematicians were using them to replace tedious multiplication. Edmund Wingate and William Oughtred are generally credited with the first slide rules around 1620 to 1630, when two logarithmically marked scales were placed side by side so that sliding one along the other turned addition of logarithms into multiplication. Oughtred also developed a circular version. Richard Delamain claimed similar ideas at about the same time, and the priority dispute is still debated.

For the next three centuries the slide rule was a working tool for engineers, surveyors, navigators, and scientists. Improvements came steadily. The cursor, a transparent window with a hairline, was added to make alignment and reading more precise. In 1859 the French artillery officer Amédée Mannheim introduced a standardized layout that became the basis for many later rules. German and Japanese makers, such as Faber-Castell and Hemmi, produced highly refined instruments in the twentieth century, including models with trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential scales.

The slide rule's popularity peaked in the decades after the Second World War. Engineering students learned to use one, and it was a familiar sight in classrooms and offices. Its decline came quickly in the early 1970s, when inexpensive electronic calculators, such as the Hewlett-Packard HP-35 in 1972, put far more capable arithmetic in a pocket. Slide rules were largely retired by the late 1970s, though they remain collectible and are still taught by some enthusiasts as a way to understand logarithms and orders of magnitude.
